lead: Shear force and bending moment diagrams are the picture of what a beam carries. This unit shows how to read a beam, find its support reactions, cut it into sections and draw the two diagrams for cantilevers, simply supported beams and overhanging beams. After it you can find SF and BM at any section, say where BM is largest, and check a diagram against the load–shear–moment relations.
about: Chapter 3.1 sets up the hardware: the supports, the reactions each one can give, and the loads — point, uniformly distributed, uniformly varying, and applied couple. Chapter 3.2 turns the beam into a free body and finds the reactions from ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0 and ΣM = 0. Chapter 3.3 uses those reactions to cut cantilevers and simply supported beams into sections and draw the shear force and bending moment diagrams. Chapter 3.4 does the same for overhanging beams, where the moment turns hogging over the support and crosses zero at a point of contraflexure. Chapter 3.5 closes the loop with w = −dV/dx and V = dM/dx, so one diagram can be checked against the other.

chapters.idea: A beam is a bar carrying transverse loads, and every support or load on it can be reduced to one of a few standard kinds.
chapters.depth: Define beam, span, and the idealisations behind them. Supports: pin (hinge) — two reactions, horizontal H and vertical V; roller — one reaction, normal to the surface; fixed — three, H, V and a moment. Some syllabi say 'simple support' for a roller and 'hinged' for a pin. Loads: point load in kN, uniformly distributed load (UDL) in kN/m over a length, uniformly varying load (UVL) in kN/m rising from zero to w, and applied couple in kN·m; add self weight as a UDL. Beam types: cantilever, simply supported, overhanging, fixed-fixed, continuous, propped cantilever. Count unknowns against the three equilibrium equations to call a beam determinate or indeterminate. State the sagging-positive sign convention in two lines only — the diagrams come later.

figure.aria: A beam model splits into three support types with their reaction counts and four load types with their units.

chapters.example: A beam 6 m long is pinned at A and rests on a roller at B at the right end. It carries a 20 kN point load 2 m from A and a UDL of 5 kN/m from A to B. Name the beam, list every unknown reaction and say whether it is statically determinate. (Answer: simply supported; 2 reactions at A plus 1 at B, so three unknowns against three equations — determinate.)
chapters.trap: Treating a roller as a pin invents a horizontal reaction that is not there; and the total of a UDL is w × L, not w — it acts at the middle of the loaded length.
chapters.prereq: First-year mechanics: force, moment of a force about a point, equilibrium of a rigid body.
chapters.leave: The arithmetic of reactions to 3.2, the diagrams to 3.3 and 3.4, and anything about fixed or continuous beams to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Replace each support by the forces it can exert, then three equilibrium equations give those forces.
chapters.depth: Steps of a free body diagram (FBD): cut the beam free, erase the supports, draw the reaction at each support in its known direction, replace each distributed load by its resultant (UDL w over L → wL at mid-length; triangular UVL → ½wL at one-third from the tall end), and show the applied loads. Then ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0 about any point. Choose the moment centre at a support so one unknown drops out; find the second reaction from ΣFy; check with a moment equation about the other support. Reaction directions: upward positive, anticlockwise positive. A plane beam with three or fewer unknowns is statically determinate — say so, and say the opposite for more, without solving those here.

figure.title: Reactions in five moves
figure.aria: A downward flow from isolating the beam to replacing supports, replacing the UDL, taking moments, summing vertical forces and checking.

chapters.example: Pin at A, roller at B, span 6 m. A 20 kN point load sits 2 m from A and a UDL of 5 kN/m covers the whole span. Find the two reactions. (Answer: ΣM about A gives R_B × 6 = 20 × 2 + 30 × 3 = 130, so R_B = 21.67 kN; ΣFy gives R_A = 50 − 21.67 = 28.33 kN.)
chapters.trap: Putting the resultant of a UDL at the wrong place (it is at mid-length, not at the support) and then forgetting the ΣFy step once the moment equation is done.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for support types and load units; first-year statics for resolving forces and taking moments.
chapters.leave: Drawing the diagrams to 3.3 and 3.4; beams with more than three unknowns go to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Cut the beam at a section, keep one side as a free body, and the shear force and bending moment at the cut follow from equilibrium of that piece.
chapters.depth: Sign convention: sagging moment positive, and shear positive when the left piece is pushed up by the right piece. Section method in four lines: take a section at distance x, keep the left part, put V (down) and M (anticlockwise) at the cut, apply equilibrium. Standard results to work out and remember: cantilever with end load — SF constant P, BM linear, P·L at the fixed end; cantilever with UDL — SF linear, BM parabolic, wL²/2 at the fixed end; simply supported with a central point load — BM peak PL/4; with a point load at distances a and b — peak Pab/L; with a UDL — BM peak wL²/8. Drawing rules: point load makes the SF jump and the BM slope kink; UDL makes the SF a straight line and the BM a parabola; BM is zero at a free end and at a simple end, and equals the fixed-end moment at a fixed end. Name the diagrams SFD and BMD.

figure.aria: Two curves along a 4 m cantilever: shear force falls in a straight line from 30 kN at the fixed end to 10 kN at the free end, while bending moment falls from 80 kN·m to zero.

chapters.example: A cantilever is fixed at A and free at B, 4 m away. A UDL of 5 kN/m runs over the whole 4 m and a 10 kN point load hangs at B. Draw the SFD and BMD and give the values at A and at B. (Answer: SF at A = 10 + 5 × 4 = 30 kN, falling to 10 kN at B; BM at A = 10 × 4 + 20 × 2 = 80 kN·m hogging, zero at B.)
chapters.trap: Sign of the moment in a cantilever — it is hogging, so negative under the sagging-positive convention — and leaving out the point load when taking the moment at the fixed end.
chapters.prereq: 3.2 for the reactions; 3.1 for beam types and the sign convention.
chapters.leave: Overhanging beams to 3.4; why M causes bending stress to Unit 4; what the beam deflects to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: An overhang carries the beam past its support, so part of the span has hogging moment and the BM curve crosses zero at a point of contraflexure.
chapters.depth: Two cases: overhang on one side and overhangs on both sides. Loads: point load on the overhang, UDL over the whole length, UDL only between the supports. Reactions from ΣM about one support, remembering the overhang load acts outside the span. Draw the SFD in the usual way; the SF crosses zero twice in general, once between the supports and once on the overhang. BM: zero at a free end, sagging maximum where V = 0 between the supports, hogging peak at the support carrying the overhang, and zero again where the curve crosses — the point of contraflexure, found by solving M(x) = 0. Find the section of zero SF by similar triangles on the straight-line SFD. State that an overhanging beam is still statically determinate.

figure.title: Working an overhang
figure.aria: A flow of steps from the whole-beam free body through each section, the hogging moment at the support, the peak sagging moment and the contraflexure point.

chapters.example: A beam is pinned at A, rests on a roller at B 4 m from A, and overhangs to a free end C, 6 m from A. A UDL of 10 kN/m acts over the whole 6 m. Find the reactions, the BM at B, the largest sagging BM and the point of contraflexure. (Answer: ΣM about A gives R_B × 4 = 60 × 3, so R_B = 45 kN and R_A = 15 kN; BM at B = −10 × 2 × 1 = −20 kN·m; SF is zero at x = 1.5 m where BM = 15 × 1.5 − 5 × 1.5² = 11.25 kN·m; M = 15x − 5x² = 0 at x = 3 m from A.)
chapters.trap: The BM at the roller support is not zero when there is an overhang, and the lever arm of an overhang load is measured from the support, not from the end.
chapters.prereq: 3.2 for reactions and 3.3 for the section method and sketch shapes.
chapters.leave: Fast checks by the area method to 3.5; continuous beams with several supports to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Load, shear force and bending moment are one family: w = −dV/dx and V = dM/dx, so areas under one curve give the changes in the next.
chapters.depth: Derive the relations on a small element of length dx carrying load w: vertical equilibrium gives dV/dx = −w, and moment equilibrium gives dM/dx = V, hence d²M/dx² = −w. Read off the consequences: the BM slope at a section equals the SF there; BM is largest or smallest where V = 0 or where V passes through zero; the change in SF between two sections equals minus the area under the load diagram; the change in BM equals the area under the SFD, sign included. Shapes: point load → SF jumps by P, BM slope kinks; concentrated couple → BM jumps by its value; UDL → SF straight, BM parabolic; UVL → SF parabolic, BM cubic. Use the area method to draw a diagram quickly and to check one already drawn.

figure.aria: On a 6 m simply supported beam under a UDL the shear force falls in a straight line from 12 kN to minus 12 kN, crossing zero at midspan, while the bending moment rises to a peak of 18 kN·m exactly at midspan and returns to zero.

chapters.example: A simply supported beam of span 6 m carries a UDL of 4 kN/m. Using V = dM/dx and the area method, find the reactions, the section where SF is zero and the largest BM, then check the BM by the area under the SFD. (Answer: R_A = R_B = 12 kN; V = 12 − 4x so V = 0 at x = 3 m; M = 12 × 3 − 4 × 3²/2 = 18 kN·m; the SF triangle has area ½ × 3 × 12 = 18 kN·m, which matches.)
chapters.trap: Signs — area under a negative SF reduces the BM, so adding magnitudes instead of signed areas gives the wrong moment at a support or an overhang.
chapters.prereq: 3.3 and 3.4, so there are diagrams to check; basic differentiation and area of a triangle and rectangle.
chapters.leave: Turning M into bending stress to Unit 4; turning M into curvature and deflection, M/EI, to Unit 5.

links: each support type becomes a known reaction on the free body
the beam type fixes the shape of the SFD and BMD
reactions are the first numbers on every diagram
the overhang adds a section beyond the support
hogging and contraflexure come straight from V = dM/dx
the area method redraws and checks the diagram
